passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Gig Economy Labour Rights

A Gig economy platforms classify workers as independent contractors delivering food, rides, or freelance tasks through smartphone applications mediating customers and labour. Companies argue flexibility attracts participants balancing caregiving or education, while labour advocates contend algorithms manage workers like employees without providing minimum wage guarantees, overtime, or collective bargaining rights. Courts in multiple jurisdictions issue conflicting rulings on employment status tests examining control, substitution, and integration into core business models. The author stresses that legal categories designed for industrial factories fit poorly with data-driven dispatch systems scaling globally. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

B Algorithmic management sets pay rates, assigns routes, and monitors acceptance metrics that implicitly discipline workers fearing deactivation for rejecting low-margin trips during rainstorms. Ratings systems create reputational precarity where a few complaints trigger account suspension without transparent appeals. Surge pricing benefits platforms and occasionally drivers, yet customers blame workers for fare spikes workers do not control. Researchers document racial and gender biases in tipping and assignment patterns inferred from names or neighbourhoods, raising anti-discrimination enforcement questions in opaque machine learning pipelines proprietors treat as trade secrets. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

C Occupational safety gaps leave couriers without employer-funded injury insurance when crashes occur rushing to meet countdown timers encouraging risky riding. Heatwaves and wildfire smoke expose outdoor workers to hazards platforms address with generic notifications rather than paid pauses. Bathroom access deficits for drivers create daily indignities seldom covered in marketing about entrepreneurial freedom. Public health studies link gig intensity to stress and sleep disruption when workers juggle multiple apps to piece together living wages below statutory minima after vehicle depreciation and fuel costs are deducted from gross earnings displayed enticingly in recruitment advertisements. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

D Collective action emerges through informal WhatsApp groups, strikes organised via social media, and nascent unions adapting to dispersed memberships without traditional shop floors. Platform cooperatives experiment with worker ownership sharing surplus, though capital requirements for technology stacks remain barriers. City ordinances mandate minimum per-minute earnings during engaged time, triggering corporate ballot initiatives spending millions to overturn protections. International labour organizations draft principles on fair data use and human review of terminations, yet enforcement across borders challenges regulators when headquarters incorporate in low-tax jurisdictions distant from streets where couriers actually labour daily. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

E Taxation systems struggle when workers deduct expenses inconsistently and lack withholding, producing year-end liabilities surprising novices. Access to mortgages and rental leases suffers without payslips, entrenching housing insecurity. Skills development is minimal when tasks are deliberately fragmented to reduce training obligations. Some workers prefer gig income as supplement to formal jobs with benefits, complicating one-size policies; others rely exclusively on platforms after factory closures in deindustrialised towns with limited alternative employment pathways beyond warehouse shifts monitored by similar algorithmic productivity scores. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

F Policy proposals include portable benefits funded by per-gig contributions, presumptive employment status unless firms prove genuine independence, and sectoral bargaining setting floors across competing apps simultaneously. Antitrust scrutiny questions whether mergers reducing platform competition harm workers through monopsony power suppressing wages. Privacy rules should govern surveillance via GPS traces and in-app microphones beyond stated purposes. The writer argues labour law modernization must centre lived experiences of couriers and cleaners, not only white-collar freelancers negotiating high-end design contracts from home offices unlike urban riders facing traffic violence hourly. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

G Looking ahead, the author believes hybrid statuses may emerge recognising flexibility while guaranteeing baseline protections portable across platforms. Without reform, taxpayers will subsidise healthcare and housing for workers formally classified as entrepreneurs. If consumers demand ethically sourced delivery, transparency about pay and safety could reshape competition beyond speed alone. Sustainable gig work requires democratic oversight of algorithms, meaningful representation, and fiscal policies treating precarious service labour as essential infrastructure rather than disposable convenience enabling urban lifestyles dependent on invisible risk-bearing at street level every rush hour. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.
